subChunks.title: Database Triggers — Automatic Reactions
subChunks.hookHtml: A trigger is a stored function that fires automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE — no application code required. Powerful and sometimes dangerous.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Anatomy of a trigger

-- Step 1: Create the trigger function
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION log_xp_change()
RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.xp != NEW.xp THEN
    INSERT INTO xp_audit (apprentice_id, old_xp, new_xp, changed_at)
    VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.xp, NEW.xp, NOW());
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;  -- RETURN NEW for BEFORE trigger; not used for AFTER
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Step 2: Attach the trigger to a table
CREATE TRIGGER trg_xp_change
AFTER UPDATE ON apprentices
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION log_xp_change();

Key concepts

  • BEFORE / AFTER — BEFORE fires before the row change (can modify NEW); AFTER fires after (cannot change the row)
  • FOR EACH ROW — fires once per affected row; FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once per statement
  • OLD / NEW — special variables in row-level triggers. OLD = row before change; NEW = row after change. INSERT has no OLD; DELETE has no NEW

Common trigger use cases

  • Audit logging — record who changed what and when
  • Maintaining derived data — auto-update a denormalised summary table
  • Enforcing complex business rules that CHECK constraints cannot express
  • Cascaded notifications

Trigger dangers

  • Invisible side effects — the trigger fires silently; developers forget it exists
  • Cascading triggers — trigger A fires trigger B fires trigger C...
  • Performance — BEFORE triggers on every INSERT/UPDATE add overhead
  • Hard to debug and test

storyBeats.text: Every time an apprentice's XP changes, an audit log must be written. The team wants this to happen automatically — no application code needed.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Triggers fire in the dark. They execute whether the change comes from the API, a migration script, or a direct SQL session. That is their strength — and their danger. Document every trigger carefully. An invisible audit log trigger is wonderful; an invisible trigger that deletes rows is catastrophic.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Trigger design

Design a trigger that automatically sets updated_at = NOW() on the apprentices table whenever a row is updated. Write: (1) the trigger function, (2) the CREATE TRIGGER statement.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
-- Step 1: Trigger function
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_updated_at()
RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := NOW();
  RETURN NEW;  -- Must return NEW in a BEFORE trigger
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Step 2: Attach to table
CREATE TRIGGER trg_set_updated_at
BEFORE UPDATE ON apprentices  -- BEFORE so we can modify NEW
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

-- Note: requires apprentices to have an updated_at column:
-- ALTER TABLE apprentices ADD COLUMN updated_at TIMESTAMP;

-- Why BEFORE: a BEFORE trigger can modify the NEW row before it is written.
-- An AFTER trigger fires after the row is committed — too late to change it.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain the difference between a BEFORE and AFTER trigger, and describe a use case where each is appropriate.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
BEFORE trigger: fires before the row is written. Can inspect and modify NEW — useful for: setting defaults (updated_at = NOW()), normalising data before insert (UPPER(name)), enforcing complex validation rules that CHECK cannot express.

AFTER trigger: fires after the row is committed to the table. Cannot change the row — useful for: audit logging (record the change after it is confirmed), propagating changes to other tables (update denormalised summary after the source changes), sending notifications.

Use BEFORE for data transformation; use AFTER for side effects.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a trigger is, the difference between BEFORE and AFTER triggers, and one example of a dangerous trigger side effect.

questions.prompt: In a row-level UPDATE trigger, what does NEW represent?
options: The row values after the UPDATE
The row values before the UPDATE
The VALUES clause of the UPDATE statement
The WHERE condition of the UPDATE
questions.answer: The row values after the UPDATE
questions.explanation: In a row-level trigger, NEW contains the row as it will look after the operation (for INSERT and UPDATE). OLD contains the row as it looked before (for UPDATE and DELETE).

questions.prompt: Why must a BEFORE trigger return NEW (not NULL or void)?
options: Returning NEW applies the (possibly modified) row to the table; returning NULL cancels the operation for that row
BEFORE triggers require a non-NULL return to confirm the row was processed
NEW must be returned for the trigger function to compile
questions.answer: Returning NEW applies the (possibly modified) row to the table; returning NULL cancels the operation for that row
questions.explanation: For row-level BEFORE triggers on INSERT and UPDATE, the return value is the row that actually gets written. RETURN NEW applies (potentially modified) row. RETURN NULL silently suppresses the row operation. RETURN NULL in a DELETE trigger cancels the delete.

questions.prompt: A trigger fires on AFTER INSERT FOR EACH ROW and tries to modify the just-inserted row. What happens?
options: It must issue an UPDATE statement — AFTER triggers cannot modify NEW directly
It can modify NEW.xp = NEW.xp + 100 and return NEW
questions.answer: It must issue an UPDATE statement — AFTER triggers cannot modify NEW directly
questions.explanation: AFTER triggers fire after the row is written. NEW can be read but modifications to it have no effect on the stored row — the row is already on disk. To modify it, you must issue an UPDATE statement inside the trigger, which may then re-fire the trigger (infinite loop risk without a guard).

questions.prompt: A developer adds a BEFORE INSERT trigger that calls an external HTTP API. What is wrong?
options: If the HTTP call fails or is slow, every INSERT is blocked or fails — this couples database write performance to an external service
BEFORE triggers cannot call external functions
The HTTP call would run outside the transaction
questions.answer: If the HTTP call fails or is slow, every INSERT is blocked or fails — this couples database write performance to an external service
questions.explanation: Database operations should be fast and predictable. An HTTP call in a trigger introduces network latency and failure modes into every row write. If the API is down, all inserts fail. Use an event queue (NOTIFY in PostgreSQL, outbox pattern) to decouple database writes from external service calls.
